html:
An eight-sided Islamic shrine on the Temple Mount in Jerusalem, finished around 691 on the orders of the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik. It is the oldest surviving major work of Islamic architecture.

It stands over the Foundation Stone, a rock that Jews hold to be the site of the Holy of Holies of their ancient Temple. Muslims connect the place with the Prophet's Night Journey to heaven. Building it there, in a city full of churches, was a statement that the new faith had arrived and meant to stay.

The design is borrowed. The octagon plan, the dome on a drum and the gold glass mosaics follow the churches of the Byzantine Empire, and local Christian craftsmen probably did much of the work. What is new is the writing. A long band of Arabic inside carries the earliest dated passages from the Quran, several of them addressed to Christians and insisting that God has no son.

The shrine belongs to the same push by Abd al-Malik that put Arabic on coins (the gold dinar) and in government. It was built during a civil war, the Second Fitna, when a rival caliph held Mecca.

Later history:

  • The crusaders made it a church in 1099.
  • Saladin restored it to Islam in 1187.
  • Suleiman the Magnificent replaced the outer mosaics with Ottoman tiles in the 1500s.
  • The gold covering of the dome dates only from the 20th century.
sum: An eight-sided Islamic shrine on the Temple Mount in Jerusalem, finished around 691 on the orders of the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik. It is the oldest surviving major work of Islamic architecture.
